record.question:
An online retailer must recover its three-tier application in a second AWS Region more than 250 miles from the primary site. The recovery time objective is 5 minutes and the recovery point objective is 1 hour. Recovery exercises show that restoring the database or provisioning the complete application tier takes longer than 5 minutes. A running reduced-capacity stack can promote its replica, scale out and switch traffic within the target.

Which strategy meets the objectives at the lowest ongoing cost among these options?

options.text: Copy hourly backups to the recovery Region. After a disaster, provision the stack with CloudFormation and restore the latest backup.
Keep only a small database replica running in the recovery Region. After a disaster, resize it and provision the web tier, application tier and load balancers.
Keep a complete reduced-capacity application stack and a continuously replicated database in the recovery Region. Automate and regularly test promotion, scale-out and traffic switching.
Keep a complete application stack with full production capacity running idle in the recovery Region, with a continuously replicated standby database.

explanation.text:
Choose <<3>>. Warm standby keeps all required tiers deployed and running at reduced capacity. The stated recovery tests establish that promotion, scaling and traffic switching fit the five-minute objective. Monitor replication lag to verify the one-hour data-loss objective as well.

<<1>> requires infrastructure creation and database restore, which the measured recovery times exclude. <<2>> is a pilot-light approach; its missing application infrastructure and database resizing also exceed the measured budget. <<4>> is full-capacity hot standby and can meet the objectives, but pays for capacity that the validated warm-standby design does not need to keep running. It is not active-active because the second Region is idle.

RTO measures time to restore the required service level. RPO measures acceptable lost data, not restart time. Strategy names do not guarantee numerical objectives: include detection, promotion, DNS or traffic propagation, scaling and application validation in recovery exercises. Select a Region pair that independently satisfies the geographic requirement.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Recovery strategy selection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html).

diagram_alt: A comparison shows which recovery tasks remain for each strategy and why tested warm standby avoids both slow provisioning and full idle capacity.

sources.supports: Warm standby keeps a complete reduced-capacity environment running; recovery objectives must be validated.

editorial_notes: Added workload-specific recovery-test results so a five-minute RTO is supported by evidence instead of a guaranteed property of warm standby.
Corrected the full-capacity passive alternative to hot standby rather than active-active.
